My published work runs along three lines: legal culture and cognition; surveillance and security infrastructures; and the measurement of crime and victimization. The two flagship pieces are a near-repeat victimization study in Almaty (*Journal of Criminal Justice*) and a comparative study of CCTV placement logics across four cities (*Journal of Computational Social Science*) — both drawing on the same underlying interest in how institutions classify space, risk and people.

![](assets/figures/schema-network.svg){width="70%" fig-alt="Schematic diagram of three overlapping cultural schema clusters, labelled law, rule and right, with unevenly distributed nodes representing individuals."}

## Peer-reviewed articles

**Serebrennikov, D.**, Minaeva, E., Ross, E. (forthcoming 2026). Surveillance as Governance: Policing Effectiveness and Political Control in the Moscow AI Experiment. *Russian Politics*. Brill. `Scopus Q1`

**Serebrennikov, D.**, Varshaver, E. (in press). Cognitive Sociology: Revisiting the Role of Cognition in Sociological Explanation. *Sociology of Power*. *(in Russian)*

**Serebrennikov, D.**, Kalkanbay, S. (2026). What's Sauce for the Goose is Sauce for the Gander? Near-repeat Victimization Across Different Urban Morphologies: Evidence from Almaty, Kazakhstan. *Journal of Criminal Justice*, 102, 102551. `Scopus Q1` — [doi.org/10.1016/j.jcrimjus.2025.102551](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcrimjus.2025.102551)

**Serebrennikov, D.**, Skougarevskiy, D. (2024). A Tale of Four Cities: Exploring Security Through Environmental Characteristics of CCTV Equipment Placement. *Journal of Computational Social Science*. — [doi.org/10.1007/s42001-024-00323-1](https://doi.org/10.1007/s42001-024-00323-1)

: Moscow, Paris, Brussels, Edinburgh: two placement logics — networked in the European cities, symbolic in Russia.

**Serebrennikov, D.** (2023). From Call to Emergency Card: Seeking "112" Operator Discretion. *Forum for Anthropology and Culture*, 59, 130–152. *(in Russian)* — [doi.org/10.31250/1815-8870-2023-19-59-130-152](https://doi.org/10.31250/1815-8870-2023-19-59-130-152)

: How emergency operators convert callers' accounts into formal incident categories — street-level classification observed as it happens.

**Serebrennikov, D.** (2023). Gaze Ex Machina: A Brief History of Police CCTV Surveillance in Russia and Western Countries. *Urban Studies and Practices*, 8(3), 101–112. *(in Russian)* — [doi.org/10.17323/usp832023101-112](https://doi.org/10.17323/usp832023101-112)

: A comparative history of police CCTV surveillance across Russia and Western countries.

**Serebrennikov, D.** (2023). Infrastructure as a Camera Obscura of Social Classifications: Urban Video Surveillance Systems in Small Cities. *Monitoring of Public Opinion*, 3. *(in Russian)* — [doi.org/10.14515/monitoring.2023.3.2325](https://doi.org/10.14515/monitoring.2023.3.2325)

: Surveillance infrastructure as a material record of official classification — what a camera system is built to see shows whom the local state treats as a suspect.

Verkeev, A., **Serebrennikov, D.** (2023). Victims of Their Own Fear: Perceived Safety and Crime Victim Experience in Russia. *Russian Sociological Review*, 22(2), 179–206. *(in Russian)* — [doi.org/10.17323/1728-192x-2023-2-179-206](https://doi.org/10.17323/1728-192x-2023-2-179-206)

: Perceived safety and actual victimization experience among crime victims in Russia.

**Serebrennikov, D.**, Khodjaeva, E., Shepeleva, O. (2023). "Street-Level Algorithm": Two Styles of Automated Law Enforcement in the Moscow "Social Monitoring" Application. *The Journal of Social Policy Studies*, 21(1), 7–24. *(in Russian)* — [doi.org/10.17323/727-0634-2023-21-1-7-24](https://doi.org/10.17323/727-0634-2023-21-1-7-24)

: The Moscow "Social Monitoring" app as behaviour converted into an offence by software, and discretion delegated from street-level bureaucrats to code.

Muravyev, A., Yuldashev, O., **Serebrennikov, D.** (2021). Surveillance Cameras in Cities: Security and Territory. *Neprikosnovenny Zapas*, 6(140), 26–41. *(in Russian)*

: Cameras as instruments of urban security and the politics of territory.

**Serebrennikov, D.**, Kuzmina, Yu. (2021). Field Experiments and the Rubin Causal Model: A Review of Approaches and Current Research. *Journal of Economic Sociology*, 22(4), 117–139. *(in Russian)* — [doi.org/10.17323/1726-3247-2021-4-117-139](https://doi.org/10.17323/1726-3247-2021-4-117-139)

: A review of field-experimental approaches to causal inference in the Rubin causal model tradition.

**Serebrennikov, D.** (2020). [Review] Ehrlich, E., Fundamental Principles of the Sociology of Law. *Sotsiologicheskiy Zhurnal*, 26(1), 183–189. *(in Russian)* — [doi.org/10.19181/socjour.2020.26.1.7059](https://doi.org/10.19181/socjour.2020.26.1.7059)

: On living law — the starting point of the work on where law exists outside the statute book.

## Preprints and datasets

Kuchakov, R., **Serebrennikov, D.**, Bobrikov, D., Knorre, A., Skougarevskiy, D. (2026). Russian Crime Victimization Survey: Pooled Cross-Sections and a Longitudinal Panel, 2018–2024. *SSRN*. — [dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6418058](https://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6418058)

: The only repeated nationwide victimization survey in Russia, now released as an open dataset: 42,572 pooled respondents across three waves (2018 / 2021 / 2024) plus a 3,456-person longitudinal panel.
